newsitem.title: USA: Boeing, McDonnell Douglas in $13.3 billion merger.
newsitem.headline: Boeing, McDonnell Douglas in $13.3 billion merger.

text.p: Aircraft titans Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas Corp said on Sunday they plan to merge and create the world's largest aerospace company in a deal worth about $13.3 billion.
"This is I believe an historic moment in aviation and aerospace," Philip Condit, who will be chairman and chief executive officer of the merged company, said at a news conference.
The companies over the years have produced the DC-3, B-52, F-15 aircraft, the Apollo capsules and the space shuttle.
The combined firm, to be based at Boeing's headquarters in Seattle and to operate under the Boeing Co name, was projected to have 1997 sales of about $48 billion, up from about $35 billion this year

The new giant would employ about 200,000 people and have a combined order backlog worth $100 billion, putting it well ahead of its nearest defense industry rival, Lockheed Martin Corp, and its nearest commercial aerospace competitor, Europe's four-nation Airbus Industrie consortium.
Company officials said any job losses would likely be minimal. There may be overlaps in some areas, Condit said, but he added: "I don't think those are going to be significant numbers."
Executives said the merger would cause "reassignments," and operations were expected to continue at existing major locations, including St Louis, where McDonnell Douglas is based.

The stock-for-stock merger must be approved by regulators and the companies hoped to complete it by mid-1997. "As soon as we get the government approval in those areas, then we'll go ahead and close the deal," Harry Stonecipher, who will be president and chief operating officer of the new firm, said.
The Justice Department declined to comment on the proposed merger.

Under the agreement, McDonnell Douglas shareholders would receive 0.65 of a share of Boeing common stock for each share of McDonnell Douglas common share. Based on Boeing's closing price of $96.75 on Friday, the companies said the deal would be worth about $13.3 billion.
Condit said the merger would be positive for shareholders, but declined to comment on what impact it would have on earnings next year.
Condit and Stonecipher shook hands on the deal at a private meeting in Seattle on Tuesday, and the merger was later approved by the respective boards of directors at each company.

"Phil and I stood up on Tuesday morning and said we have a basis for a deal that we are willing to take to our boards, and we shook hands," Stonecipher said. The final deal came together late on Saturday afternoon, he added.
Speculation of a possible merger swirled after an announcement earlier this month that Boeing agreed to hire McDonnell Douglas as a subcontractor on future wide-body aircraft.
"We have common cultures," Stonecipher said. "We have a common vision of where we're trying to go and I think we can get there faster together than we could separately," he added.

The merger will leave Airbus Industrie as the only other major player in the business of making large commercial aircraft. An Airbus spokesman said McDonnell Douglas has not been a competitor in the civilian aircraft business for a number of years "so it hasn't altered the equation in the commercial field at all for Airbus."

McDonnell Douglas has long been viewed as the sick man of the commercial aerospace industry, having seen much of its business in the civil aircraft area stolen away by Airbus, which was formed 25 years ago.
Boeing has the lead position in the civil aircraft industry, while McDonnell Douglas is the third-largest commercial aircraft company.

"I use the word balance," Condit said. "They (McDonnell Douglas) were heavily defense, a lot smaller on the commercial side. Boeing is very strong on the commercial side, a lot smaller on the defense side," he said.

Of the $48 billion in projected 1997 sales, about $34 billion would be from Boeing and $14 billion from McDonnell Douglas. A Boeing spokesman had earlier said the split was $28 billion from Boeing and $20 billion from McDonnell Douglas.

Major U.S. airlines said it was too soon to forecast the impact of the proposed merger on airliner prices or their airplane-buying strategies. "It is too early to tell," Delta Air Lines Inc spokesman Todd Clay said.
